description: Immediate physiological responses and the long-term training adaptations of the body systems.
content_html:
Two Timescales of Change

Exercise affects the body across two distinct timescales in OCR’s specification, and your ability to distinguish between them is frequently tested. Short-term effects occur during the exercise session itself and in the hours immediately after it — they are temporary and reverse once the body has recovered. Long-term effects emerge only after months or years of consistent training and represent genuine physiological adaptation — the body has permanently restructured itself to cope more efficiently with the demands of regular exercise. Mixing these up in an exam will cost marks, so developing a clear mental map of which changes belong to which category is essential.

Short-Term Effects: What Happens During and Immediately After Exercise

As exercise begins, several changes are immediately measurable. Muscle temperature rises as the working muscles generate heat, increasing the speed of metabolic reactions and making the muscle tissue more pliable. Heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output all increase, responding to the greater demand for oxygen-carrying blood in the working muscles. Heart rate may climb from around 70 bpm at rest to 180 bpm or more during maximal effort, while stroke volume rises as the ventricles fill more completely and contract more forcefully.

A particularly important short-term effect for OCR is the redistribution of blood flow during exercise. The body redirects a greater proportion of cardiac output to the working skeletal muscles and the heart muscle itself, while blood supply to the digestive system and other non-essential organs is reduced. This ensures the muscles receive the oxygen and glucose they need during activity. Breathing rate and tidal volume both increase, raising minute ventilation to supply more oxygen to the lungs and remove carbon dioxide more rapidly. Oxygen delivery to the working muscles increases accordingly, supporting aerobic energy production. Where exercise intensity rises beyond the aerobic threshold, lactic acid production accelerates as the body supplements aerobic energy production with anaerobic pathways.

Key Fact

OCR’s six short-term effects of exercise: (1) increased muscle temperature; (2) increased heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output; (3) redistribution of blood flow during exercise; (4) increased breathing rate, tidal volume and minute ventilation; (5) increased oxygen delivery to the working muscles; (6) increased lactic acid production. All of these reverse when exercise stops.

Long-Term Effects: Adaptations From Months of Training

Consistent exercise over months and years causes permanent physiological adaptations across multiple body systems. These long-term effects represent the body becoming structurally and functionally more efficient at the demands placed on it. OCR’s specification names a broader set of long-term adaptations than many other boards — all named adaptations below must be known precisely.

Muscular and Skeletal Adaptations

Regular resistance training produces hypertrophy of the skeletal muscles — the muscle fibres grow larger, producing greater strength and power. Muscular endurance improves as the muscles become better at sustaining repeated contractions without fatiguing. Closely linked is improved resistance to fatigue: trained muscles are more efficient at using oxygen and fuel, and can delay lactic acid accumulation, meaning they can sustain high-intensity effort for longer before performance declines. Bone density increases with weight-bearing exercise, making bones stronger and more resistant to injury — a benefit that also protects against conditions such as osteoporosis in later life. Muscular strength increases as hypertrophy and neuromuscular recruitment both improve.

Cardiovascular Adaptations

Two of the most significant long-term cardiovascular adaptations are hypertrophy of the heart and a reduction in resting heart rate. The heart grows larger and stronger as a muscle in response to the repeated demands of training. A larger, stronger heart can pump a greater volume of blood per beat — a greater resting stroke volume. Because resting stroke volume is higher, the heart does not need to beat as many times per minute to deliver the same cardiac output, resulting in a permanently lower resting heart rate (a long-term adaptation sometimes called bradycardia). While the average untrained person has a resting heart rate of around 60–80 bpm, elite endurance athletes such as cyclists or distance runners may have resting heart rates of 35–50 bpm.

Capillarisation is another important cardiovascular adaptation. Regular endurance training stimulates the growth of new capillaries in and around the trained muscle groups, increasing capillary density. This improves oxygen delivery to the muscle fibres and speeds up the removal of carbon dioxide and waste products. The overall cardiac output (the maximum amount the heart can pump per minute) also increases with training, as both maximum heart rate is maintained and maximum stroke volume rises. The result is a significantly higher aerobic capacity — the maximum rate at which oxygen can be consumed and used by the muscles during maximal exercise. Finally, rate of recovery improves: a trained athlete’s heart rate returns to resting values more quickly after effort, a sign of cardiovascular efficiency.

A very common exam error is placing a long-term adaptation in the short-term column, or vice versa. “Increased heart rate” is a short-term effect — it happens during a single exercise session and reverses immediately after. “Hypertrophy of the heart” is a long-term effect — it takes months of consistent training to develop. Similarly, “increased breathing rate” is short-term, while “strengthened respiratory muscles” is long-term. When answering exam questions, always state the timescale explicitly: “in the short term, heart rate increases during the session” vs “in the long term, after months of training, the heart undergoes hypertrophy.”

Respiratory Adaptations

The respiratory muscles — primarily the diaphragm and intercostal muscles — become stronger with regular training, enabling larger tidal volumes and more forceful, efficient breathing. This means trained athletes can ventilate their lungs more effectively at high exercise intensities, maintaining a strong concentration gradient at the alveoli even under heavy muscular demand. Tidal volume and minute ventilation during exercise increase as the respiratory muscles adapt, allowing more air to be moved per breath and per minute.

Key Fact

The chain: regular training → hypertrophy of the heart (the heart grows larger) → greater resting stroke volume per beat → lower resting heart rate needed to maintain cardiac output. Also: training → capillarisation → improved oxygen delivery to muscle fibres → improved aerobic capacity and resistance to fatigue.

Consider a club cyclist who has been training consistently for two years. In the long term, her heart has undergone hypertrophy, so her stroke volume at rest is around 90 ml compared to the untrained average of 70 ml. Her resting heart rate has dropped from 74 bpm to around 56 bpm. Her muscles have become more capillarised, delivering more oxygen per unit time to her quadriceps and hamstrings. Her respiratory muscles are stronger, and her resistance to fatigue has increased, meaning she can sustain a high power output for longer before lactic acid forces her to ease off. Her aerobic capacity (VO2 max) has improved substantially, and her rate of recovery between efforts has shortened. All of these are the result of systematic, progressive training over months — not a single session.
exam_tip_html: The most common error on questions about effects of exercise is confusing the two timescales. Short-term effects occur during or immediately after exercise — they are temporary. Long-term effects take months or years of consistent training to develop. In “describe” and “explain” questions, always state the timescale explicitly: “in the long term, after months of training, the heart undergoes hypertrophy, which leads to a lower resting heart rate.” For the 8-mark “Evaluate” question, go beyond listing: connect the adaptation to a named component of fitness and then to a sporting performance benefit. For example: “Capillarisation increases the density of capillaries in the quadriceps, improving oxygen delivery, which improves cardiovascular endurance and allows a county cyclist to sustain a higher pace over a 40 km time trial without fatigue.” The data-handling questions in this topic require you to quote a figure from the table, describe what it shows, and explain the sporting implication — all three steps are needed for full marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Short-term effects of exercise include increased muscle temperature, raised heart rate/stroke volume/cardiac output, redistribution of blood flow to working muscles, increased breathing rate and tidal volume, greater oxygen delivery to muscles, and increased lactic acid production during high-intensity effort.
  • Long-term cardiovascular adaptations include hypertrophy of the heart, higher resting stroke volume, lower resting heart rate, improved cardiac output, increased capillarisation and faster rate of recovery.
  • Long-term muscular and respiratory adaptations include hypertrophy of skeletal muscles, improved muscular endurance, greater resistance to fatigue, increased bone density, stronger respiratory muscles and improved aerobic capacity.

practice_questions.text: Identify one short-term effect of exercise on the cardiovascular system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: increased heart rate; increased stroke volume; increased cardiac output; redistribution of blood flow to working muscles. Accept equivalent physiological descriptions.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'capillarisation' as a long-term effect of exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying capillarisation as the growth of new capillaries in and around trained muscle tissue; 1 mark for stating that this increases capillary density and improves oxygen delivery to the muscle fibres (or: improves the removal of waste products such as CO2).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows resting heart rate data for three athletes before and after a 6-month endurance training programme.

Athlete | Resting HR before (bpm) | Resting HR after (bpm)
Amira   | 74                      | 59
Ben     | 70                      | 57
Chloe   | 76                      | 62

Calculate the mean reduction in resting heart rate across all three athletes. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly calculating each individual reduction (Amira: 15 bpm; Ben: 13 bpm; Chloe: 14 bpm); 1 mark for summing correctly (15 + 13 + 14 = 42 bpm) and dividing by 3; 1 mark for the correct final answer: 14 bpm (accept 14.0). Units required (bpm) for the final answer mark.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows heart rate and stroke volume data at rest and during a 10 km race for a trained distance runner.

Condition     | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
At rest       | 52               | 88
During race   | 185              | 118

Calculate the cardiac output at rest and during the race, and interpret what the data tells you about the runner's cardiovascular fitness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct resting cardiac output: Q = 52 × 88 = 4,576 ml/min; 1 mark for correct race cardiac output: Q = 185 × 118 = 21,830 ml/min; 1 mark for a valid comparison (e.g. cardiac output increases approximately 4.8 times during the race compared with rest, from 4,576 to 21,830 ml/min); 1 mark for a sporting interpretation (e.g. the low resting heart rate of 52 bpm suggests long-term cardiac hypertrophy, with a high stroke volume of 88 ml at rest indicating an efficient, trained heart capable of meeting the greatly elevated oxygen demand during the 10 km). If calculations are incorrect but method is sound, award 1 mark for working and 1 mark for a valid interpretation of their figures.

practice_questions.text: Explain how hypertrophy of the heart leads to a lower resting heart rate in a trained endurance athlete.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining hypertrophy of the heart as the long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle due to regular training; 1 mark for explaining that this means the heart can pump a greater stroke volume per beat; 1 mark for explaining that a higher stroke volume means the heart beats fewer times per minute to deliver the same cardiac output; 1 mark for naming a lower resting heart rate as the result (accept: bradycardia; state that it is typically below 60 bpm in trained athletes). Full marks require the logical chain to be clear.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level netball player has been following a structured 8-month fitness programme. Evaluate the short-term and long-term effects this programme is likely to have had on her cardiovascular and respiratory systems, and explain how these effects could improve her performance on court.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Full range of short-term and long-term effects covered with accuracy. Short-term: increased heart rate/stroke volume/cardiac output during matches; redistribution of blood flow to working muscles; increased breathing rate and tidal volume; increased oxygen delivery; lactic acid production during explosive efforts. Long-term: hypertrophy of the heart; lower resting heart rate (with mechanism explained); increased resting stroke volume and cardiac output; capillarisation improving oxygen delivery to muscles; stronger respiratory muscles; improved aerobic capacity; better rate of recovery; improved resistance to fatigue. Each adaptation linked to a specific netball performance benefit (e.g. capillarisation supports sustained running in attack/defence; lower resting heart rate means she recovers faster between high-intensity passages of play; stronger respiratory muscles support higher minute ventilation during intense defensive sets). Evaluation includes at least one limitation or counter-argument (e.g. long-term adaptations take months and are reversible if training stops; short-term fatigue can temporarily impair performance; genetic ceiling on cardiac output). Justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6 marks): Most cardiovascular and respiratory effects covered with reasonable accuracy; most applied to netball; some evaluation; conclusion reached.

Developing (3-4 marks): Short-term or long-term effects described but not both; limited sporting application to netball; one-sided.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic reference to heart rate increasing during exercise or the heart getting bigger; limited application or evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a LONG-TERM effect of regular endurance training?
What does 'capillarisation' mean as a long-term effect of exercise?
options: The heart grows larger and stronger
Lactic acid is produced more efficiently
New capillaries grow in trained muscle tissue, increasing oxygen delivery

knowledge_checks.q: Redistribution of blood flow during exercise means more blood is directed towards _____ muscles.
An anticipatory rise in heart rate before exercise begins is triggered by the release of _____.
Match each effect of exercise to the correct timescale:
right: Short-term (during or after a single session)

flashcard_questions.q: Name the six short-term effects of exercise on the body.
flashcard_questions.a: Increased muscle temperature; raised HR/SV/cardiac output; redistribution of blood flow; increased breathing rate/tidal volume; more oxygen to muscles; increased lactic acid production.
The long-term growth of new capillaries in trained muscle tissue, increasing oxygen delivery and waste removal.

flashcard_questions.q: What is hypertrophy of the heart?
flashcard_questions.a: The long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle caused by regular training, enabling a greater stroke volume.

flashcard_questions.q: Explain the link: hypertrophy of the heart → lower resting heart rate.
flashcard_questions.a: Bigger heart pumps greater stroke volume per beat, so fewer beats are needed per minute to deliver the same cardiac output.
The maximum rate at which the body can consume and use oxygen during maximal exercise; it improves with long-term training.

flashcard_questions.q: What is resistance to fatigue as a long-term effect?
flashcard_questions.a: Trained muscles can sustain effort for longer before lactic acid accumulates and performance declines.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does redistribution of blood flow matter during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: It channels a greater share of cardiac output to working muscles, increasing oxygen delivery during activity.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two long-term effects of training on the respiratory system.
flashcard_questions.a: Stronger respiratory muscles; improved tidal volume and minute ventilation during exercise. (Also: increased aerobic capacity.)

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to bone density as a long-term effect of weight-bearing exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Bone density increases, making bones stronger and more resistant to injury.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two long-term effects on the muscular system.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: hypertrophy; increased muscular strength; improved muscular endurance; greater resistance to fatigue.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the rate of recovery as a long-term adaptation?
flashcard_questions.a: A trained athlete's heart rate returns to resting values more quickly after exercise, a sign of cardiovascular efficiency.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a lower resting heart rate in a trained athlete tell you about their heart?
flashcard_questions.a: Their heart has undergone hypertrophy (grown larger), producing a higher stroke volume per beat.

glossary_terms.definition: The long-term increase in the size of the heart muscle, particularly the left ventricle, resulting from regular sustained exercise training.
The growth of new capillaries into and around trained muscle tissue as a result of regular exercise, increasing capillary density and improving oxygen delivery.
The maximum rate at which the body can consume and use oxygen during maximal exercise; it increases as a long-term effect of endurance training.
A long-term training adaptation in which muscles become better at sustaining effort before lactic acid accumulation causes performance to decline.
The increase in the cross-sectional size of individual muscle fibres as a result of progressive resistance training, producing greater muscle bulk and strength.
A short-term effect of exercise in which cardiac output is redirected towards the working muscles and away from non-essential organs such as the digestive system.
The speed at which heart rate and breathing rate return to resting values after exercise; it improves as a long-term effect of training.
The volume of blood ejected by one ventricle per heartbeat; resting stroke volume increases as a long-term adaptation to endurance training.

hero_image_caption: Regular training produces lasting adaptations to the heart, muscles and respiratory system.
